parole.testo: Likely onomatopoeic. Appears to contain the frequentative suffix -eren. An early etymology suggesting that it may ultimately represent a derivation from Proto-Germanic *heufaną (via an unattested Middle Dutch *hūven) is today generally dismissed as implausible.

Compound of mee (“madder”) + krap (“hook”). The first element is inherited from Middle Dutch mede, which derives from Proto-Germanic *maiþǭ. The second element was likely added in reference to hook-shaped parts of the plant. First attested as meecrappe in 1588, although Middle Dutch already has crap
From Middle Dutch nie, from Old Dutch nie, from Proto-Germanic *ne *aiwaz. Cognate to German nie. Equivalent to n- (“n-”) + ie (“ever”) (from Middle Dutch ie, from Old Dutch io).

A merger of two related verbs: * Middle Dutch rinnen (“to flow, to run fast”), from Old Dutch *rinnan, from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną. * Middle Dutch rennen (“to run/ride fast”), from Old Dutch *rennen, from Proto-Germanic *rannijaną. Doublet with runnen (“to manage”).
